Q: Selecting particular elements from a list of lists A:

Simply use distributional::parameters():

dd %>%
  dplyr::bind_cols(parameters(.$GPRT))

#> # A tibble: 4 × 6
#>   .model          yemo         GPRT .mean    mu sigma
#>   <chr>          <mth>       <dist> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 ARIMA(GPRT) 2024 Dec  N(136, 853)   136   136  29.2
#> 2 ARIMA(GPRT) 2025 Jan N(136, 1225)   136   136  35  
#> 3 ARIMA(GPRT) 2025 Feb N(136, 1399)   136   136  37.4
#> 4 ARIMA(GPRT) 2025 Mar N(135, 1482)   135   135  38.5

If you want them in a separate dataframe:

parameters(dd$GPRT)

#>    mu sigma
#> 1 136  29.2
#> 2 136  35.0
#> 3 136  37.4
#> 4 135  38.5

Rather educational R core:

dd$GPRT |>
  rapply(unclass) |> # unlist()
  stack() |>
  unstack()

   mu sigma
1 136  29.2
2 136  35.0
3 136  37.4
4 135  38.5

dd$GPRT |>
  unclass() |>
  do.call(what='rbind')

     mu  sigma
[1,] 136 29.2 
[2,] 136 35   
[3,] 136 37.4 
[4,] 135 38.5 

dd$GPRT |>
  unclass() |>
  lapply(unclass) |>
  list2DF()

1  136 136  136  135
2 29.2  35 37.4 38.5

Data

library(distributional)

dd <- tibble::tibble(
  .model = "ARIMA(GPRT)",
  yemo = tsibble::yearmonth(c("2024 Dec", "2025 Jan", "2025 Feb", "2025 Mar")),
  GPRT = dist_normal(mu = c(136, 136, 136, 135), 
                     sigma = c(29.2, 35, 37.4, 38.5)),
  .mean = c(136, 136, 136, 135)
)

Created on 2026-02-08 with reprex v2.1.1

Q: Vim clear last search highlighting A:

Based on @baruch-even answer, you can delete search term on ESC double press while in normal mode with:

nnoremap <esc> :let @/ = ""<return><esc>
nnoremap <esc>^[ <esc>^[

Q: How to get script directory in POSIX sh? A:

The POSIX-shell (sh) counterpart of $BASH_SOURCE is $0. see bottom for background info

Caveat: The crucial difference is that if your script is being sourced (loaded into the current shell with .), the snippets below will not work properly. explanation further below

Note that I've changed DIR to dir in the snippets below, because it's better not to use all-uppercase variable names so as to avoid clashes with environment variables and special shell variables.
The CDPATH= prefix takes the place of > /dev/null in the original command: $CDPATH is set to a null string so as to ensure that cd never echoes anything.

In the simplest case, this will do (the POSIX equivalent of the OP's command):

dir=$(CDPATH= cd -- "$(dirname -- "$0")" && pwd)

If you also want to resolve the directory path to its ultimate target in case the directory and/or its components are symlinks, add -P to the pwd command:

dir=$(CDPATH= cd -- "$(dirname -- "$0")" && pwd -P)

Caveat: This is NOT the same as finding the script's own true directory of origin:
Let's say your script foo is symlinked to /usr/local/bin/foo in the $PATH, but its true path is /foodir/bin/foo.
The above will still report /usr/local/bin, because the symlink resolution (-P) is applied to the directory, /usr/local/bin, rather than to the script itself.

To find the script's own true directory of origin, you'd have to inspect the script's path to see if it's a symlink and, if so, follow the (chain of) symlinks to the ultimate target file, and then extract the directory path from the target file's canonical path.

GNU's readlink -f (better: readlink -e) could do that for you, but readlink is not a POSIX utility.
While BSD platforms, including macOS, have a readlink utility too, on macOS it doesn't support -f's functionality. That said, to show how simple the task becomes if readlink -f is available:
dir=$(dirname "$(readlink -f -- "$0")").

In fact, there is no POSIX utility for resolving file symlinks. There are ways to work around that, but they're cumbersome and not fully robust:

The following, POSIX-compliant shell function implements what GNU's readlink -e does and is a reasonably robust solution that only fails in two rare edge cases:

  • paths with embedded newlines (very rare)
  • filenames containing literal string -> (also rare)

With this function, named rreadlink, defined, the following determines the script's true directory path of origin:

dir=$(dirname -- "$(rreadlink "$0")")

Note: If you're willing to assume the presence of a readlink utility - which would cover macOS, FreeBSD and Linux - a similar, but simpler solution can be found in this answer to a related question.

rreadlink() source code - place before calls to it in scripts:

rreadlink() ( # Execute the function in a *subshell* to localize variables and the effect of `cd`.

  target=$1 fname= targetDir= CDPATH=

  # Try to make the execution environment as predictable as possible:
  # All commands below are invoked via `command`, so we must make sure that `command`
  # itself is not redefined as an alias or shell function.
  # (Note that command is too inconsistent across shells, so we don't use it.)
  # `command` is a *builtin* in bash, dash, ksh, zsh, and some platforms do not even have
  # an external utility version of it (e.g, Ubuntu).
  # `command` bypasses aliases and shell functions and also finds builtins 
  # in bash, dash, and ksh. In zsh, option POSIX_BUILTINS must be turned on for that
  # to happen.
  { \unalias command; \unset -f command; } >/dev/null 2>&1
  [ -n "$ZSH_VERSION" ] && options[POSIX_BUILTINS]=on # make zsh find *builtins* with `command` too.

  while :; do # Resolve potential symlinks until the ultimate target is found.
      [ -L "$target" ] || [ -e "$target" ] || { command printf '%s\n' "ERROR: '$target' does not exist." >&2; return 1; }
      command cd "$(command dirname -- "$target")" # Change to target dir; necessary for correct resolution of target path.
      fname=$(command basename -- "$target") # Extract filename.
      [ "$fname" = '/' ] && fname='' # !! curiously, `basename /` returns '/'
      if [ -L "$fname" ]; then
        # Extract [next] target path, which may be defined
        # *relative* to the symlink's own directory.
        # Note: We parse `ls -l` output to find the symlink target
        #       which is the only POSIX-compliant, albeit somewhat fragile, way.
        target=$(command ls -l "$fname")
        target=${target#*' -> '}
        continue # Resolve [next] symlink target.
      fi
      break # Ultimate target reached.
  done
  targetDir=$(command pwd -P) # Get canonical dir. path
  # Output the ultimate target's canonical path.
  # Note that we manually resolve paths ending in /. and /.. to make sure we have a normalized path.
  if [ "$fname" = '.' ]; then
    command printf '%s\n' "${targetDir%/}"
  elif  [ "$fname" = '..' ]; then
    # Caveat: something like /var/.. will resolve to /private (assuming /var@ -> /private/var), i.e. the '..' is applied
    # AFTER canonicalization.
    command printf '%s\n' "$(command dirname -- "${targetDir}")"
  else
    command printf '%s\n' "${targetDir%/}/$fname"
  fi
)

To be robust and predictable, the function uses command to ensure that only shell builtins or external utilities are called (ignores overloads in the forms of aliases and functions).
It's been tested in recent versions of the following shells: bash, dash, ksh, zsh.

Note that an enhanced version of this function is available as a downloadable utility, rreadlink; use it with the -e option. If you have Node.js installed, you can install it with [sudo] npm install rreadlink -g

How to handle sourced invocations:

tl;dr:

Using POSIX features only:

  • You cannot determine the script's path in a sourced invocation (except in zsh, which, however, doesn't usually act as sh).

  • You can detect whether or not your script is being sourced ONLY if your script is being sourced directly by the shell (such as in a shell profile/initialization file; possibly via a chain of sourcings), by comparing $0 to the shell executable name/path (except in zsh, where, as noted $0 is truly the current script's path). By contrast (except in zsh), a script being sourced from another script that itself was directly invoked, contains that script's path in $0.

  • To solve these problems, bash, ksh, and zsh have nonstandard features that do allow determining the actual script path even in sourced scenarios and also detecting whether a script is being sourced or not; for instance, in bash, $BASH_SOURCE always contains the running script's path, whether it's being sourced or not, and [[ $0 != "$BASH_SOURCE" ]] can be used to test whether the script is being sourced.

    • This answer indirectly shows these techniques, in the context of determining whether a given script is being sourced.

To show why this cannot be done, let's analyze the command from Walter A's answer:

    # NOT recommended - see discussion below.
    DIR=$( cd -P -- "$(dirname -- "$(command -v -- "$0")")" && pwd -P )
  • (Two asides:
    • Using -P twice is redundant - it's sufficient to use it with pwd.
    • The command is missing silencing of cd's potential stdout output, if $CDPATH happens to be set.)
  • command -v -- "$0"
    • command -v -- "$0" is designed to cover one additional scenario: if the script is being sourced from an interactive shell, $0 typically contains the mere filename of the shell executable (sh), in which case dirname would simply return . (because that's what dirname invariably does when given a argument without a path component). command -v -- "$0" then returns that shell's absolute path through a $PATH lookup (/bin/sh). Note, however, that login shells on some platforms (e.g., OSX) have their filename prefixed with - in $0 (-sh), in which case command -v -- "$0" doesn't work as intended (returns an empty string).
    • Conversely, command -v -- "$0" can misbehave in two non-sourced scenarios in which the shell executable, sh, is directly invoked, with the script as an argument:
      • if the script itself is not executable: command -v -- "$0" may return an empty string, depending on what specific shell acts as sh on a given system: bash, ksh, and zsh return an empty string; only dash echoes $0
        The POSIX spec. for command doesn't explicitly say whether command -v, when applied to a filesystem path, should only return executable files - which is what bash, ksh, and zsh do - but you can argue that it is implied by the very purpose of command; curiously, dash, which is usually the most compliant POSIX citizen, is deviating from the standard here. By contrast, ksh is the lone model citizen here, because it is the only one that reports executable files only and reports them with an absolute (albeit not normalized) path, as the spec requires.
      • if the script is executable, but not in the $PATH, and the invocation uses its mere filename (e.g., sh myScript), command -v -- "$0" will also return the empty string, except in dash.
    • Given that the script's directory cannot be determined when the script is being sourced - because $0 then doesn't contain that information (except in zsh, which doesn't usually act as sh) - there's no good solution to this problem.
      • Returning the shell executable's directory path in that situation is of limited use - it is, after all, not the script's directory - except perhaps to later use that path in a test to determine whether or not the script is being sourced.
        • A more reliable approach would be to simply test $0 directly: [ "$0" = "sh" ] || [ "$0" = "-sh" ] || [ "$0" = "/bin/sh" ]
      • However, even that doesn't work if the script is being sourced from another script (that was itself directly invoked), because $0 then simply contains the sourcing script's path.
    • Given the limited usefulness of command -v -- "$0" in sourced scenarios and the fact that it breaks two non-sourced scenarios, my vote is for NOT using it, which leaves us with:
      • All non-sourced scenarios are covered.
      • In sourced invocations, you cannot determine the script's path, and at best, in limited circumstances, you can detect whether or not sourcing is occurring:
        • When sourced directly by the shell (such as from a shell profile/initialization file), $dir ends up either containing ., if the shell executable was invoked as a mere filename (applying dirname to a mere filename always returns .), or the shell executable's directory path otherwise. . cannot be reliably distinguished from a non-sourced invocation from the current directory.
        • When sourced from another script (that was itself not also sourced), $0 contains that script's path, and the script being sourced has no way of telling whether that's the case.

Background information:

POSIX defines the behavior of $0 with respect to shell scripts here.

Essentially, $0 should reflect the path of the script file as specified, which implies:

  • Do NOT rely on $0 containing an absolute path.

  • $0 contains an absolute path only if:

  • you explicitly specify an absolute path; e.g.:

    • ~/bin/myScript (assuming the script itself is executable)
    • sh ~/bin/myScript

  • you invoke an executable script by mere filename, which requires that it both be executable and in the $PATH; behind the scenes, the system transforms myScript into an absolute path and then executes it; e.g.:

    • myScript # executes /home/jdoe/bin/myScript, for instance

  • In all other cases, $0 will reflect the script path as specified:

    • When explicitly invoking sh with a script, this can be a mere filename (e.g., sh myScript) or a relative path (e.g., sh ./myScript)
    • When invoking an executable script directly, this can be a relative path (e.g., ./myScript - note that a mere filename would only find scripts in the $PATH).

In practice, bash, dash, ksh, and zsh all exhibit this behavior.

By contrast, POSIX does NOT mandate the value of $0 when sourcing a script (using the special built-in utility . ("dot")), so you cannot rely on it, and, in practice, behavior differs across shells.

  • Thus, you cannot blindly use $0 when your script is being sourced and expect standardized behavior.
    • In practice, bash, dash, and ksh leave $0 untouched when sourcing scripts, meaning that $0 contains the caller's $0 value, or, more accurately, the $0 value of the most recent caller in the call chain that hasn't been sourced itself; thus, $0 may point either to the shell's executable or to the path of another (directly invoked) script that sourced the current one.
    • By contrast, zsh, as the lone dissenter, actually does report the current script's path in $0. Conversely, $0 will provide no indication as to whether the script is being sourced or not.
    • In short: using POSIX features only, you can neither tell reliably whether the script at hand is being sourced, nor what the script at hand's path is, nor what the relationship of $0 to the current script's path is.
  • If you do need to handle this situation, you must identify the specific shell at hand and access its specific non-standard features:
    • bash, ksh, and zsh all offer their own ways of obtaining the running script's path, even when it's being sourced.

For the sake of completeness: the value of $0 in other contexts:

  • Inside a shell function, POSIX mandates that $0 remain unchanged; therefore, whatever value it has outside the function, it'll have inside as well.
    • In practice, bash, dash, and ksh do behave that way.
    • Again, zsh is the lone dissenter and reports the function's name.
  • In a shell that accepted a command string via the -c option on startup, it's the first operand (non-option argument) that sets $0; e.g.:
    • sh -c 'echo \$0: $0 \$1: $1' foo one # -> '$0: foo $1: one'
    • bash, dash, ksh, and zsh all behave that way.
  • Otherwise, in a shell not executing a script file, $0 is the value of the first argument that the shell's parent process passed - typically, that's the shell's name or path (e.g. sh, or /bin/sh); this includes:
    • an interactive shell
      • Caveat: some platforms, notably OSX, always create login shells when creating interactive shells, and prepend - to the shell name before placing it in $0, so as to signal to the shell that it is a _login shell; thus, by default, $0 reports -bash, not bash, in interactive shells on OSX.
    • a shell that reads commands from stdin
      • this also applies to piping a script file to the shell via stdin (e.g., sh < myScript)
    • bash, dash, ksh, and zsh all behave that way.

Q: How can I create a database for a MongoDB container on startup? A:

Steps to create multiple databases and users in a MongoDB Docker container without root access.

  1. Stop Docker Compose with the

    docker-compose down

    command, or 'docker-compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.dev.yml <...>' if you have multiple files.

  2. Remove volumes assigned to the MongoDB container. Run 'docker volume ls'. If there is anything similar to <projectfolder>_mongodb--vol, remove it by applying

    docker volume rm <projectfolder>_mongodb--vol

  3. Set up the folder for the mongo database with .js or .sh init scripts. For example, mongo-init/db_1.js:

    conn = new Mongo();
db = conn.getDB("db_1")
db.createUser(
{
    user: "db_1_service_user",
    pwd: "<password>",
    roles: [
        {
            role: "readWrite",
            db: "db_1"
        }
    ]
}
);

    Repeat the procedure for the mongo-init/db_2.js file. conn.getDB() creates the database, and db.createUser() creates a user and assigns it to the database.

  4. File docker-compose.yml fragment. Notice the mount binding from ./mongo-init/ local folder containing database init scripts to the remote /docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/:

    version: "3.8"
services:

  my-service_1:
    depends_on:
      - mongodb

  my-service_2:
    depends_on:
      - mongodb

  mongodb:
    image: mongo:4.4-bionic
    ports:
    - "27017:27017"
    volumes:
    - mongodb--vol:/data/db
    - ./mongo-init/:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/:ro
    healthcheck:
    test: "echo 'db.runCommand(\"ping\").ok'"
    interval: 5s
    timeout: 5s
    retries: 3

# In-service volumes are very slow in macOS and Windows,
# so use fast shared volumes for large storage
volumes:
    mongodb--vol:

  5. Apply connection strings to your applications:

    mongodb://db_1_service_user:<password>@mongodb:27017/db_1

    mongodb://db_2_service_user:<password>@mongodb:27017/db_2

Q: Avalonia DataGrid - Horizontal scrolling cuts off cells when RowHeight is less than 20 A:

TL;DR If you simply want your table rows to be 18px tall without any glitches, then do this:

  • Setting <DataGrid RowHeight="18" will only set the DataGrid's default DataGridRow.DesiredSize to 18, but you also need to set other values too.
  • You also need to override Avalonia's Fluent.xaml' ControlTheme for DataGridCell (and DataGridColumnHeader too, for consistency); specifically, set:
    • Change MinHeight from the default of 32 (I use 16, to account for 1px borders along top and bottom edges).
    • Lower FontSize below the default of 15.
  • ...as both of these properties will keep your DataGridCell sizes above 18px in height.

Like so:

<DataGrid
    RowHeight="18"
    ItemsSource="{Binding People}"
    AutoGenerateColumns="True"
    IsReadOnly="True"
    GridLinesVisibility="All"
>
    <DataGrid.Resources>
        <ControlTheme x:Key="{x:Type DataGridCell}" TargetType="DataGridCell">
            <Setter Property="MinHeight" Value="16" />
            <Setter Property="FontSize"  Value="10" />
        </ControlTheme>
        <ControlTheme x:Key="{x:Type DataGridColumnHeader}" TargetType="DataGridColumnHeader">
            <Setter Property="MinHeight" Value="16" />
            <Setter Property="FontSize"  Value="10" />
        </ControlTheme>
    </DataGrid.Resources>

</DataGrid>

...gives me this, with no glitches when scrolling horizontally:

Now for the details...

Before continuing, I recommend first reading Parts 1 and 2 of The Avalonia Book available online.

Why doesn't <DataGrid RowHeight=""> just-work?

  1. (For reference, the StyledProperty definition of RowHeight="" in <DataGrid> is defined here).

  2. Contrary to intuition, the RowHeight="" value is used by DatagridCellsPresenter as the basis for the desired row-height - and is not necessarily taken as a hard limit on row height under all circumstances, which means that any contained content in table cells exceeding the row-height could cause the actual rendered row-height to exceed the specified RowHeight="" value.

    • In fact, that's actually what happens in your code, but this is mitigated by Avalonia's default clipping behaviour - more on that later.

  3. So while <DataGrid RowHeight=""> constrains the row height, it doesn't constrain the cell height.

  4. ...and that's because the Fluent theme you're using sets its own MinHeight on all DataGridCell instances by default:

    <ControlTheme x:Key="{x:Type DataGridCell}" TargetType="DataGridCell">
    <!-- etc -->
    <Setter Property="FontSize" Value="15" />
    <Setter Property="MinHeight" Value="32" />

  5. If you were to fire-up Avalonia's F12 legacy dev-tools - or the much more powerful (and free-for-30-days) new "Pro" DevTools) then you'll see that despite appearances, the DataGridCell is actually 32px tall yet lives in a 19px tall DataGridRow.

...so this explains why (without any scrolling yet) the RowHeight="18" is ignored and the rows are rendered with an actual height of 32px.

Why is it that only the cells in the first column get clipped, and only after you start horizontally-scrolling the DataGrid?

It's caused by behaviour in Avalonia's DataGrid's "frozen column" functionality (DataGridCellPresenter.ArrangeOverride and EnsureCellClip):

y'see, DataGrid has support for a frozen-first-column, just like in Excel and other DataGrids: so that any row-headers in Column 0 will remain on-screen while the user scrolls to the right - just like how column headers (i.e. Row 0) remain "frozen" on-screen while you scroll down a long, tall table.

Now, supposing Column 0 is frozen to its leftmost position in the visible DataGrid and the user has now started scrolling to the right: that means that the cells in Column 1 will be partially occluded by Column 0 (because Column 1 slips behind Column 0 as the user scrolls, followed by Column 2 slipping behind Column 0, then Column 3, and so on).

...in order to render the current partially-occluded column the DataGridCellPresenter (DGCP) sets a Clip region on all cells in that column. Then, as the column moves off-screen as the user scrolls the DGCP then removes the Clip from the now-offscreen column and applies it to the next column.

Note that multiple columns can be on-screen and occluded by the frozen column (e.g. if the frozen Column 0 is 200px wide, while Columns 1, 2, 3 and 4 are each 50px wide): supposing the horizontal scroll-position is now 190px then the first 3 columns will be fully occluded and will have a Clip mask covering their whole dimensions, while Column 4 will have a 10px slither still visible, while Columns 5 and beyond will not be clipped.

...this case (of not clipping subsequent columns) is handled by DataGridCellPresenter.EnsureCellClip: if the current cell's column's left-edge is beyond the frozenLeftEdge then it sets cell.Clip = null, thus removing all clips.

Specifically, see DataGridCellsPresenter.EnsureCellClip, when EnsureCellClip is called with (for example) these args: ( cell, ..., frozenLeftEdge: 0, cellLeftEdge: 67 ) then the cell.Clip will be set only when frozenLeftEdge > cellLeftEdge

  • ...but, for-all columns to the right of the partially-occluded leftmost column, ( frozenLeftEdge > cellLeftEdge ) == false, so cell.Clip = null.
  • ...so occluded columns get clipped, all columns to the right of those don't get clipped.
  • ...and in this particular project, there will never be more than 1 occluded column, but other projects may vary.

...but my original post has nothing to do with frozen columns! How is this relevant?

I think this might be a bug in Avalonia - at the same time it might not be: y'see, conceptually it-can-be-said that there's no difference between these 3 cases:

  1. When Column 0 is Frozen and is 200px wide, and Column 1 is sliding underneath it as the user scrolls, partially occluding it.
  2. When Column 0 is Frozen and is 0px wide, and Column 1 is sliding underneath it as the user scrolls, partially occluding it.
  3. When Column 0 is not frozen; but the user is still scrolling to the right so much that Column 0 is now entirely off-screen and Column 1 is now partially off-screen.

...and in the 3rd case, the DGCP is still applying a Clip to those cells in Column 1; though I feel it's unnecessary, but combining the cases probably does simplify the code because it doesn't need to check for that condition specifically? I'unno.

I say it might be a bug because the .Clip rectangle is sized for the DataGridRow but not the DataGridCell.

But also: I don't see why the clipping is necessary at all anyway: I'd have thought that simply reordering the cells in the Z-axis (such that Frozen Columns have a higher Z-index than non-frozen columns) would be sufficient.

So to re-cap so far:

  1. Under all conditions (i.e. when the DataGrid's horizontal-scroll-position is 0 or >= 1; or whether or not any columns are frozen), the DataGridCellPresenter will check if the leftmost cell in its row is partially-occluded by either a frozen-column or because the leftmost cell's column is partially scrolled off-screen.
    1. If the cell is occluded, then it applies a Clip to the cell based on the DesiredRowHeight and not the cell's actual height if it so-happens to exceed the DesiredRowHeight.
    2. If the cell is not occluded then DGCP will not set a Clip and will clear any currently set clip.

This explains why no cells are clipped until you start scrolling, and why it only affects the leftmost column's cells.

So... the bugs (so-far) are:

  • DGCP should use the DataGridCell's actual layout-height for its Clip rectangle's height and not the DesiredRowHeight.
  • Using <DataGrid RowHeight="" alone is insufficient for setting a smaller maximum row-height. You must also override the current theme/style's defined sizes but also address other theme/style-defined content sizes, such as font-size, padding, margins, and border width, because those all add-up to produce other effective minimum heights of their own.
    • Specifically, in Fluent.xaml, the <ControlTheme> for DataGridCell should have the following properties overridden:
      • <Setter Property="FontSize" Value="15" />
      • <Setter Property="MinHeight" Value="32" />
    • Ditto for DataGridColumnHeader's <ControlTheme> properties too.

...wait a second! But my rows are 18px tall - not 32px, and the clipped cells appear shorter than 18px - that doesn't add-up with what you just wrote!

Actually, it does - it only looks like it doesn't....

Here's what I see on my computer, and those DataGridRow elements are indeed 18px 19px tall:

100% Zoom 800% Zoom

(It's 19px because the 18px RowHeight="" is combined with a 1px tall horizontal border between each row, this is set on PART_BottomGridLine).

However, even though each DataGridRow is 19px, each DataGridCell in each row is actually 32px, but is vertically-centred within the 18px viewport (so there's 7px beyond the top and bottom edges of the DataGridRow that's hidden):

...and that 32px comes from the <Setter Property="MinHeight" Value="32" /> in Fluent.xaml.

Let's summarize this new information:

  • The <DataGrid RowHeight="18"> sets a limit on the size of DataGridRow.

  • The Fluent.xaml defines a MinHeight="32" on DataGridCell.

  • When a DataGridCell element is taller than its DataGridRow then it gets centred and clipped by the DataGridRow.

    • Note that this "clipping" of DataGridCell is not using DataGridCell's .Clip property; instead it's because the DataGridRow' has its own ClipToBounds property set to true.
      • When an Avalonia parent element has ClipToBounds it's basically the the same thing as using HTML's overflow: hidden on a 100x100px fixed-size element which contains a 200x200px fixed-size child element.

  • Separately, I want to describe how .Clip works, briefly: Avalonia, like any UI or visual system, has two main concerns:

    1. The "layout" of components, based on content-sizes (be they fixed-sizes, constraints, and more),
    2. The rendering or "painting" of those components on-screen once their layout is calculated.
    • In contrast to WinForms - and (everyday) HTML+CSS - the "layout-size" of an element in Avalonia can be different to the "render size" of the same element. A bright pink rectangle element might be sized at 500x1500px - but it doesn't necessarily have to be rendered like that on-screen: a 50x50px-sized square .Clip rectangle can be positioned at the top-left corner of the pink rectangle, which would mean only a 50x50px pink square would appear on-screen, followed by 450x1450px of emptiness until the user scrolls down to the next laid-out element.
    • i.e. using a clipping mask/region will crop an element;
    • In Avalonia, when a .Clip rectangle is defined, it's applied or positioned relative to the top-left corner of its .Bounds (i.e. the top-left-corner of its layout box).

Now...

  1. ...recall back to how DataGridCellPresenter will apply a Rectangular .Clip to any DataGridCell elements in the leftmost column when partially occluded.
  2. ...and the .Clip rectangle's height is the same as the <DataGrid RowHeight="" value (18px).
  3. ...and that .Clip is applied from the top-left corner of the DataGridCell (which is 32px tall).
  4. ...and that the DataGridCell, being 32px tall, is vertically centered in an 18px tall DataGridRow with .ClipToBounds set.
  5. ...which means the .Clip rectangle itself will be partially obscured by the DataGridRow's bounds.
  6. ...which explains exactly what you originally observed!

It is demonstrable, by looking at the bounding-box of the DataGridCell of the middle DataGridRow below. For clarity I made the other 4 rows fully transparent, and disabled DataGridRow.ClipToBounds so that you can see the full (post-.Clip) DataGridCell which would otherwise be cropped even more:

As you can see, the post-clip size of DataGridCell is 18px tall, from the top-left corner, such that it slices through half of the TextBlock of the cell, which is exactly what we expect - and what you saw.

Appendix 2: Alternatives:

Alternative 1: Use Simple.xaml:

Because Fluent.xaml's minimum cell height is integral to the problem, one alternative is to swap out Fluent.xaml for the other in-box style: Simple.xaml, which doesn't look all that bad - and doesn't glitch-out either:

To do this, just change your App.xaml like so:

<Application
    xmlns       = "https://github.com/avaloniaui"
    xmlns:x     = "http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml"
    x:Class     = "AvaloniaDataGridExample.App"
    xmlns:local = "using:AvaloniaDataGridExample"
>
    <!--
        "Default" ThemeVariant follows system theme variant. "Dark" or "Light" are other available options.
        RequestedThemeVariant = "Default"
    -->

    <Application.Styles>

        <SimpleTheme  />
        <StyleInclude Source="avares://Avalonia.Controls.DataGrid/Themes/Simple.xaml"/>
        <!--
        <FluentTheme DensityStyle="Normal" />
        <FluentTheme DensityStyle="Compact" />
        <StyleInclude Source="avares://Avalonia.Controls.DataGrid/Themes/Fluent.xaml"/>
        -->
    </Application.Styles>
</Application>

I removed the RequestedThemeVariant="" attribute as it seems unnecessary for me, but YMMV.

Alternative 2: Use Fluent.xaml's DensityStyle="Compact":

Documented here.

However, I compared them both and they came out identical - it seems DataGrid does not have feature any different styles or metrics when using DensityStyle=""Compact, though most of the other built-in controls do (like Textboxes, ComboBoxes, ListBox and ListView, etc)

Q: How can I run a native MongoDB query in MongoDB Compass? A:

MongoDB Compass provides the console at very bottom to run your query as you can run in the command line. You can just write your query after clicking on the ">_ MONGOSH":

Something like:

db.yourcollection.find({id: {$eq: "00"}}).pretty()
